content: In the field of mathematical sciences, a stationary process, also referred to as a strictly stationary process or strongly stationary process, is a type of stochastic process. The defining characteristic of such a process is that its joint probability distribution remains invariant when shifted in time or space. Consequently, statistical parameters such as the mean and variance, provided they exist, do not change over time or position. Stationarity is a critical concept in time series analysis. Often, raw data are transformed to achieve stationarity. For instance, economic data frequently exhibit seasonal patterns or dependencies on price levels, and these characteristics are adjusted to render the data stationary. Processes are described as trend stationary if they can be expressed as a linear combination of a stationary process and one or more processes that exhibit a trend. The act of transforming data to remove trends, leaving a stationary dataset for analysis, is known as de-trending. Formally, let ( X_t ) represent a stochastic process, and let ( F_{X_{t_1}, ldots, X_{t_k}}(x_{t_1}, ldots, x_{t_k}) ) denote the cumulative distribution function of the joint distribution of ( X_t ) at times ( t_1, ldots, t_k ). The process ( X_t ) is considered stationary if, for all ( k ), for all ( tau ), and for all ( t_1, ldots, t_k ), the joint distribution remains unchanged under time shifts. As an example, white noise is a stationary process. In contrast, the sound of a cymbal crash is not stationary because the acoustic power of the crash, and therefore its variance, diminishes over time. A discrete-time stationary process with a discrete sample space, where the random variable can take on one of ( N ) possible values, is exemplified by a Bernoulli scheme. Other examples of discrete-time stationary processes include autoregressive and moving average signals. A weaker form of stationarity, commonly used in signal processing, is known as weak-sense stationarity (WSS), wide-sense stationarity, second-order stationarity, or covariance stationarity. WSS random processes require only that the first and second moments (mean and covariance) do not vary with time. Any strictly stationary process that has a mean and covariance is also WSS. For a continuous-time random process ( x(t) ) that is WSS, the following conditions must hold: 1. The mean function ( m_x(t) ) must be constant over time. 2. The correlation function must depend only on the time difference between ( t_1 ) and ( t_2 ), and thus can be indexed by a single variable rather than two. Instead of expressing the correlation function in terms of two variables, it is typically abbreviated to depend on the time difference alone. When processing WSS random signals using linear, time-invariant (LTI) filters, the correlation function can be treated as a linear operator. Since this operator is circulant (depending only on the difference between its two arguments), its eigenfunctions are Fourier complex exponentials. Furthermore, because the eigenfunctions of LTI operators are also complex exponentials, the processing of WSS random signals with LTI systems is highly tractable. All computations can be efficiently performed in the frequency domain. As a result, the WSS assumption is widely utilized in signal processing algorithms due to its mathematical convenience and practical applicability.
